bank <- bank[ , -c(1, 5)]
str(bank)

bank$Education <- as.factor(bank$Education)
bank$Securities.Account <- as.factor(bank$Securities.Account)
bank$CD.Account <- as.factor(bank$CD.Account)
bank$Online <- as.factor(bank$Online)
bank$CreditCard <- as.factor(bank$CreditCard)

bank <- bank[, c(setdiff(names(bank), "Personal.Loan"), "Personal.Loan")]

train_df$Personal.Loan <- as.factor(train_df$Personal.Loan)  # Replace with your target column name
valid_df$Personal.Loan <- as.factor(valid_df$Personal.Loan)  # Replace with your target column name

train_features <- train_df[, -which(names(train_df) == "Personal.Loan")]  # Replace with your target column name
train_target <- train_df$Personal.Loan  # Now a factor
valid_features <- valid_df[, -which(names(valid_df) == "Personal.Loan")]
valid_target <- valid_df$Personal.Loan  # Now a factor

install.packages("caret")  
install.packages("kknn")
library(caret)
library(kknn)
#Perform k-NN classification for k = 3
knn3 <- train(train_features, train_target, method = "knn", tuneGrid = data.frame(k = 3), 
              trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10))
knn3_pred <- predict(knn3, valid_features)
knn3_pred <- factor(knn3_pred, levels = levels(valid_target))
confusionMatrix(knn3_pred, valid_target)
knn3 <- train(train_features, train_target, method = "knn", tuneGrid = data.frame(k = 3), trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10))
knn3_pred <- predict(knn3, valid_features)
confusionMatrix(knn3_pred, valid_target)

#Perform k-NN classification for k = 5

knn5 <- train(train_features, train_target, method = "knn", tuneGrid = data.frame(k = 5), 
              trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10))
knn5_pred <- predict(knn5, valid_features)
knn5_pred <- factor(knn5_pred, levels = levels(valid_target))
confusionMatrix(knn5_pred, valid_target)

#Perform k-NN classification for k = 7

knn7 <- train(train_features, train_target, method = "knn", tuneGrid = data.frame(k = 7), 
              trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10))
knn7_pred <- predict(knn7, valid_features)
knn7_pred <- factor(knn7_pred, levels = levels(valid_target))
confusionMatrix(knn7_pred, valid_target)

    I selected k = 7 for my k-NN classification model because it achieved the highest sensitivity, at 0.997265. Sensitivity measures the model's ability to correctly identify true positives, in this case, predicting the class of non-loan takers accurately. I think it should be crucial to select a model that minimizes false negatives and maximizes the correct identification of this majority class. 

    3.Predictions in the validation set
    
install.packages("caret")  
install.packages("kknn")
library(caret)
library(kknn)
  knn_pred_k7_valid <- predict(knn7, valid_features)
confusionMatrix(knn_pred_k7_valid, as.factor(valid_df$Personal.Loan), positive = "1")  # Adjust "1" based on your target classes
library(ROSE)
roc_curve <- ROSE::roc.curve(valid_df$Personal.Loan, 
                              knn_pred_k7_valid, 
                              plot = TRUE, 
                              main = "ROC Curve for k-NN (k = 7)")
cat("Area Under the Curve (AUC):", roc_curve$auc, "\n")
  
  Accuracy: The accuracy of the model is 91.2%, which means that the model correctly predicts the class for 91.2% of the validation instances. However, a high accuracy can also lead to imbalance datasets. A model that always predicts class 0 (non-loan takers) would still achieve 99% accuracy, but it wouldn’t correctly identify any loan takers at all. Therefore, high accuracy may show the fact that the model is failing to identify important cases in the minority class.
  
  Sensitivity: With a sensitivity of 99.7%, the model is highly effective at predicting the majority class (non-loan takers), correctly identifying nearly all of them. This aligns with my goal to minimize false negatives for the majority class.
  
  Specificity: Specificity is extremely low at 0.005814, which indicates that the model struggles to correctly identify the minority class (loan takers, class 1). This means the model fails to distinguish loan takers, resulting in a very high false positive rate for class 1.
  
  Balanced Accuracy: The Balanced Accuracy (0.501539) is a measure that accounts for both sensitivity and specificity. Since specificity is low, balanced accuracy is just over 50%, reflecting the model's bias toward the majority class.
  
  Conclusion: While the model performs well in terms of sensitivity and accuracy, it has a serious bias towards class 0 (non-loan takers), as indicated by its very low specificity. The model's overall accuracy is high, but this is primarily due to the imbalance in the data, with many more non-loan takers than loan takers. In summary, I believe the model is good at predicting non-loan takers but performs poorly in identifying loan takers, making it less effective if the goal is to predict loan approval accurately. If my goal is to predict loan-takers, I would need more improvement in this model by trying to address the class imbalance.
